title: Chermoula baked fish
skill: Checking a fillet and baking it to 145°F

notes.text: For more than 4, use two baking dishes on the same rack, or a sheet pan, so the fillets sit in one layer with space around them.

move.title: A green paste, a gentle oven
move.body: Chermoula is a Moroccan paste of cilantro, parsley, garlic, cumin, paprika, lemon, and olive oil, used on fish all along the coast. You'll check the fillets for pin bones by feel, coat them in chermoula, and bake them on sliced tomatoes until they flake and reach 145°F. Fish goes from done to dry in a couple of minutes, so you'll start checking early. Cod is leaner than salmon, so it dries out faster.

why.title: Feel before you cook
why.body: Pin bones are thin bones that sit in a line along the thick end of a fillet. Most cod is sold boned, but a few get missed. Running a fingertip along the fillet finds them in seconds, and they pull out cleanly before cooking, not in someone's mouth.

why.title: Pat it dry
why.body: Fish straight from the package is wet on the surface. A wet fillet steams in its own water, and the paste slides off. Patting it dry lets the chermoula cling and the top roast instead of stew.

why.title: Short time in the lemon
why.body: Lemon juice is an acid, and acid starts to firm the outside of raw fish, the way heat does. Fifteen minutes flavors it. An hour or more turns the surface chalky and soft. Fish takes a short marinade; tough meat can take a long one.

why.title: Tuck the thin end
why.body: A cod fillet is thick at one end and thin at the other, so the tail end is done long before the middle. Folding the thin end under makes the whole piece about the same thickness, so it all reaches 145°F together.

why.title: Opaque, flaking, 145°F
why.body: Raw fish is shiny and see-through. As it cooks, its proteins set and it turns opaque white, and the flakes start to separate when pressed. Those are signs; the thermometer in the thickest part, at 145°F, is the proof.

wrong.sign: The fish is dry and falls apart
wrong.fix: It went past 145°F. Spoon the tomatoes and their juice over it to serve. Next time, start checking 3 minutes sooner.

wrong.sign: It's 145°F at the edges but under it in the middle
wrong.fix: Put it back for 2 minutes and check the thickest part again.

wrong.sign: You find a bone while eating
wrong.fix: Set it aside on your plate. Next time, run your fingertip along the thick end in both directions before cooking.
The garlic was in big pieces, or there wasn't enough oil. Stir a spoonful of olive oil into the leftover paste and serve it on the side.

quiz.q: Where do you feel for pin bones?
choices: Along the middle of the thick end
quiz.explain: Pin bones sit in a line through the thickest part.

quiz.q: Why is the fish only in the lemony paste for 15 minutes?
choices: Acid firms the outside, and too long turns it chalky
quiz.explain: Fish needs only a short time in acid.

quiz.q: Why fold the thin end of the fillet under?
choices: So the whole piece is about the same thickness and cooks evenly
So it fits in the dish
quiz.explain: The thin end would be done long before the thick part.

quiz.q: What tells you for sure the fish is done?
quiz.explain: Opaque and flaking are good signs; the thermometer is the proof.

substitutions.note: Tilapia fillets are thinner, so start checking for 145°F after 10 minutes.

steps.text: Put a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 400°F.

Wash the lemon, cilantro, and parsley, and dry the herbs well. Grate the yellow zest off the lemon on the fine holes of the grater into the small bowl, then halve the lemon and squeeze in its juice, catching the seeds.
Gather the cilantro and parsley into a tight pile and chop them fine, about ⅛ inch, rocking the knife. Peel and mince the garlic. Add both to the bowl.
steps.look: Fine green flecks with no whole leaves.

steps.text: Stir the cumin, paprika, cayenne if you're using it, the chermoula's salt, and the olive oil into the bowl until it's a loose, spoonable paste.

Core the tomatoes and slice them into ¼-inch rounds. Halve the onion piece and slice it into thin half-moons. Spread both in the baking dish, pour the tomatoes' oil over them, and sprinkle with the tomatoes' salt.

Lay the cod on the paper towels on a plate. Run a fingertip slowly along the middle of each thick end, both ways, feeling for hard tips. Pull out any you find with the tweezers, toward the head end, at the angle the bone lies. Pat the fillets dry on both sides.
Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands and the tweezers with soap.
Sprinkle the fish's salt over the fillets. Spoon half the chermoula over them and spread it over the tops and sides with the back of the spoon. Leave them on the plate.
Lay the fillets on the tomatoes with the spatula, 1 inch apart. Fold the thin end of each one under so the piece is an even thickness. Spoon the rest of the chermoula over the top.
steps.look: Every piece about 1 inch thick, from end to end.

steps.text: Wash your hands, the spoon, and the spatula, and put the raw-fish plate in the sink.
Bake the fish until it's opaque white and starts to flake when you press the thickest part with a fork.
steps.look: No shiny, see-through flesh in the middle.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the side of the thickest fillet. It needs to read at least 145°F. If it doesn't, bake 2 more minutes and check again.
While the fish rests in the dish for 2 minutes, slice the baguette with the bread knife.
Lift each fillet onto a plate with the spatula, and spoon the tomatoes and their juice beside it. Serve with the bread to soak up the juice.
